CS3005 Topic 6 - 2D Graphics

2D Graphics: Text

Text can either be formatted, unformatted or hypertext.

Unformatted Text

  • Also known as plain text.
  • Can be encoded in ASCII or Unicode / UTF.
    • ASCII is a 256-character encoding common in programming.
    • Unicode aims to provide uniform character encoding and is common everywhere else

Formatted Text

  • Includes text types such as tables, columns, equations, or even simple formatting like underlining.
  • Font sizes, types and effects also count as formatting text.

Hypertext

  • Interactive text that performs an action when e.g. clicked on, such as links.

2D Graphics: Images

Images can be represented in a vector format or a raster format.

Vector Images allow for:

  • Infinite Zoom
  • Scalable file size based on number of paths

Raster Images allow for:

  • Limited zoom
  • Scalable file size based on resolution of image in pixels.

Vector formats include PDFs, SVGs, EPSs
Raster formats include BMPs, PNGs, JPEGs

Anti-Aliasing

Attempts can be made to transition the edges of pixels to minimize the jagged effect seen in raster imaging.

Image Types

Monochrome Images

  • Known as 1-bit images.
  • Each pixel is either black or white; the image contains no colour, represented by a 0 or 1 on a pixel grid.

Grayscale Images

  • Rather than storing a 0 or 1, each pixel stores a value between 0 and 255
  • Each pixel is represented by a single byte
  • The resolution of a grayscale image is the number of pixels it contains e.g. HD is 1920x1080
  • To find the megapixel rating you can multiply the L and W
  • Grayscale images require more storage than monochrome images, but less than 24-bit colour images

24-Bit Colour Images

  • Image data stored as one bit per colour (Red, Green, Blue)
  • Computer screens can only technically display these colours, even if we had infinite bits per colour.

RGB and CMYK

  • RGB is an additive colour model (screens have a black background) and is used mainly in digital imagery.
  • CMYK is a subtractive colour model (starts with a white background) and is supported by printers/for physical media.
    • Some digital media tools support CMYK as well to enable print previews.
    • We use black to allow for a fourth, grayscale pixel value to be encoded.

24-Bit is known as 'true' colour as it is said to be able to represent all the colours we see with the human eye.

Note: Many '24-Bit Colour' images are actually stored as 32-bit to account for another value - transparency.

Indexed Colour

  • Old consoles will typically use a table in memory representing a colour index, known as a palette or colour table.
  • This is seen in consoles such as the NES.
    • Each pixel is 1-byte-encoded to represent a value on the colour palette.

Image File Types - Raster (Summary)

JPEG
  • 'Joint Photographic Experts Group'
  • Lossy compression format for images.
  • Discrete cosine transforms provide this compression.
  • JPEGs can have a user-set quality
  • Poorly compressed JPEGs can contain 'blocky' artifacts.
GIF
  • 'Graphics Interchange Format'
  • 8-bit colour palettes selected from a 24-bit colour space
  • Animated GIFs have one palette per frame.
  • Uses Lempel-Ziv-Welch lossless compression, which works well for repeating patterns.
PNG
  • 'Portable Network Graphics'
  • Attempts to supersede GIFs in all ways except animation.
  • PNGs can support up to 48 bits of colour information per pixel.
TIFF
  • 'Tagged Image File Format'
  • Allows for the attachment of extra information i.e. tags to images for extra flexibility.
  • TIFFs can store many different encodings such as 1-bit grayscale all the way up to 24-bit RGB, etc.
  • TIFF is lossless, but tags exist now to provide JPEG style compression.
  • TIFFs are common in printing and publishing.

Image File Types - Vector (Summary)

PS/PDF

  • Vector-based imaging language
  • PostScript includes text and vector-structured graphics.
SVG
  • Supports vector graphics, shapes and text

Animations

  • An animation is an image designed to change over time.
  • They can exist in 2D or 3D (creating a depth illusion)

Animation Types

Moving Object
Objects are placed on the screen and then controlled by a software program

Image Replacement
Entities are animated by changing in between frames in a sprite set.

Zoom/Resize
Object boundaries changed under program control.

Rotoscoping

Colour-Cycle Animation
Colour component values are modified.

Keyframing/Inbetweening

  • Keyframes are drawings that define the start and end positions of an animated object.
  • Programs can interpolate the frames between two keyframes in order to create effective animation.

Animation File Formats

GIF and GIFV
  • GIFs can be animated, but oftentimes compression is of poor quality.
  • GIFV is now used more often, but it is not a video file.
APNG
  • Animated version of PNGs, similar to GIFs.
  • On non-supported platforms, the first frame is written as a PNG stream allowing for display.
WEBP
  • Animation format supporting lossy and lossless compression methods.
  • Kind of garbage, doesn't outperform APNG or JPEG.

2D Graphics: Audio

Audio Types

  • Static audio includes ongoing game audio such as background music.
  • Dynamic audio is everything else:
    • Interactive audio is triggered by player actions.
    • Adaptive audio is triggered by changes in the gameplay environment, not player actions directly.
